v: Before Calgary had a name, this place already had three. In Blackfoot, Stoney, and Tsoo-tee-na, they all mean the same thing: the elbow.
This is the story of Calgary's First Peoples.
For at least eight thousand years, people have lived where the Bow and Elbow rivers meet.
The Blackfoot Confederacy: Siksika, Kainai, and Piikani. The Tsoo-tee-na, who speak a Dene language. The Stoney Nakoda, people of the mountains. And the May-tee, who wintered along the Bow.
Life followed the buffalo. Families moved with the seasons, used every part of the animal, and set careful fires to renew the grass that drew the herds.
Their homes left marks you can still see. On Nose Hill, stone circles that once held down lodge covers still rest in the grass.
In eighteen seventy-seven, the five Nations made Treaty Seven with the Crown. The Elders say it was a treaty of peace, and of sharing the land.
Then came hard years. By eighteen seventy-nine, the buffalo were gone. For more than a century, children were sent to residential schools, ten of them in and around Calgary.
But the Nations held on to their languages, their ceremonies, and their stories.
Since the first Stampede in nineteen twelve, Treaty Seven families have raised painted tipis by the Elbow River. Some designs are hundreds of years old.

In twenty fourteen, Nations from both sides of the border signed the Buffalo Treaty, to bring the buffalo home. In twenty seventeen, sixteen bison returned to Banff. Today, the herd is over one hundred.
The Kainai Nation is building Canada's first fire guardians program, bringing good fire back to heal the prairie.
In twenty nineteen, Writing-on-Stone, a sacred Blackfoot place of rock art, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Today, more than forty-eight thousand Indigenous people live in the Calgary region. Next door, the Tsoo-tee-na Nation is building Taza, with shops, hotels, and entertainment along Tsoo-tee-na Trail.
Long before it was Calgary, it was the elbow. Their story is Calgary's story. calgary insight dot c a.
